name: Linear scleroderma en coup de sabre

clinicalPearls: A subtype of linear morphoea presenting as a linear, atrophic, sclerotic band on the frontoparietal scalp and forehead, likened to the stroke of a sabre.
Predominantly affects children and young adults and follows the lines of Blaschko, suggesting cutaneous mosaicism.
Overlaps with Parry-Romberg progressive hemifacial atrophy, which may represent a severe end of the same spectrum.
May extend beyond skin into subcutaneous tissue, muscle and underlying bone, producing facial asymmetry.
Neurological complications include seizures and headache, with ipsilateral white-matter change, calcification and atrophy seen on MRI.
Ocular and dental or orofacial abnormalities may occur on the affected side.
It is a localised, not systemic, sclerosing disorder, so Raynaud phenomenon and internal organ sclerosis are absent.
Active disease is treated with immunosuppression such as methotrexate with or without systemic corticosteroids, while established deformity may need later reconstructive surgery.
reference.pathophysiology: En coup de sabre is a form of localised scleroderma in which immune activation drives fibroblast stimulation, excessive collagen deposition and progressive sclerosis and atrophy of skin and deeper tissues in a linear, Blaschko-distributed segment of the face and scalp. Postulated mechanisms include autoimmune-mediated microvascular injury and inflammation, with possible roles for cutaneous mosaicism and, in some, antecedent trauma or infection as triggers; contiguous involvement of underlying structures accounts for the bony atrophy and neurological findings.
additionalDifferentials: Lupus panniculitis and discoid lupus erythematosus
Scleroderma-like conditions such as porphyria or graft-versus-host disease
additionalInvestigations: Autoantibody profile including antinuclear antibodies to characterise autoimmunity
MRI brain for intracranial involvement when neurological symptoms are present
MRI of the affected soft tissue and face to assess depth of involvement
Inflammatory markers to gauge disease activity
Ophthalmological and dental or maxillofacial assessment
Serial clinical photography with a validated skin activity score
redFlags: New seizures or focal neurological signs
Progressive extension across the midline or rapid deepening of the lesion
Involvement threatening growth of the facial skeleton in a child
reference.prognosis: The disease often becomes inactive over years but leaves permanent atrophy and asymmetry; early immunosuppression can limit progression, while neurological and ocular involvement determine additional morbidity.
pitfalls: Mistaking it for systemic sclerosis and pursuing unnecessary internal-organ investigation.
Delaying immunosuppression during the active inflammatory phase and allowing avoidable deformity.
Overlooking the overlap with Parry-Romberg syndrome.
Attempting reconstructive surgery before the disease is quiescent.
references: Consensus guidance on juvenile localised scleroderma (morphoea)
management: Institute systemic immunosuppression during active disease, with methotrexate, frequently combined with systemic corticosteroids, to halt progression of sclerosis and atrophy
Use mycophenolate mofetil or other immunosuppressants for refractory or progressive disease
Provide physiotherapy and topical measures to maintain soft-tissue mobility and skin condition
Monitor disease activity clinically and with inflammatory markers and imaging to guide duration of immunosuppression
Undertake neurological surveillance with brain MRI where seizures or headache occur, treating seizures with antiseizure medication
Arrange ophthalmology and dental or maxillofacial assessment for the ocular and orofacial complications on the affected side
Offer reconstructive intervention such as autologous fat grafting or corrective surgery for established atrophy and asymmetry once disease is inactive
Coordinate care across dermatology, rheumatology and neurology
